name: Borders, Oil and War: The Modern Middle East
description: From the end of the Ottoman Empire to the Arab Spring: how new states, oil and a series of wars shaped the region over the last century.

checkpoints.name: The fading empire
checkpoints.note: The Suez Canal opened in 1869, and Zionism, a movement for a Jewish homeland, began in 1897. The Ottoman Empire entered the First World War and fought at Gallipoli in 1915, and after defeat Mustafa Kemal Ataturk led Turkey's fight for independence.

checkpoints.name: New states
checkpoints.note: The Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 settled the borders of the new Turkey. After the First World War Britain and France took charge of the former Ottoman Arab lands as mandates, and the lines they drew became the borders of Iraq, Syria and Palestine. Iraq gained independence and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was proclaimed in 1932.

checkpoints.name: Israel, Egypt and the wars
checkpoints.note: David Ben-Gurion declared Israel's independence in 1948, and the 1948 Arab-Israeli War followed. In Egypt, a republic from 1953, Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal, leading to the Suez Crisis of 1956, and in 1967 Israel won the Six-Day War.

checkpoints.name: Oil and revolution
checkpoints.note: The oil crisis of 1973 showed the power of oil producers. The Camp David Accords, brokered by Jimmy Carter, brought peace between Egypt and Israel, while Yasser Arafat's PLO kept the Palestinian cause at the centre. In 1979 the Iranian Revolution brought Khomeini to power, followed by another oil shock, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran-Iraq War.

checkpoints.name: A new century of war
checkpoints.note: Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait, which led to the Gulf War of 1991. After the September 11 attacks came the war in Afghanistan and in 2003 the Iraq War. The Arab Spring began in 2010, and the Syrian civil war followed.
